text.p: Australian retail sales fell 1.0 percent in December and posted a fall of 1.3 percent in real terms over the December quarter, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
Market forecasts had centred on a 0.5 percent rise in the monthly data and a 0.5 percent fall in quarterly real terms.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows.
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"There's no doubt that today's data for December confirms a picture of weak retail spending in the December quarter. In terms of the overall picture for consumer spending ... we really won't know what that looks like until the December quarter national accounts are released on March 5."
RIC SIMES, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ROTHSCHILD AUSTRALIA:

"The retail numbers are weaker than markets expected ... but a weak period was largely factored into most people's thinking. As to what the bank will do, my reading is that they've always wanted to conduct monetary policy looking 12 to 18 months out. That's why they cut twice at the end of last year. They were expecting a weak period over Christmas and New Year and wanted to provide some stimulus. I don't think today is fundamentally different from what they were thinking."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"The data is totally consistent with the very gloomy news that we have seen from some of the larger retailers for several months now, so in some respects we shouldn't be totally surprised. The retail sector is one area of the economy which is not only below potential, it's really very much in the doldrums. It needs the impact of these rate cuts we've seen to bite, and is the one sector that clearly is still supporting the case for a rate cut and keeps the chance alive."
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"The seasonality between December and January in retail sales is always a bit suspect given the shifting time of post Christmas sales and the tendency of consumers to defer spending until after Christmas. But on balance, this would be a figure that adds to the case for a further rate cut."
CRAIG JAMES, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"If they are still meeting at the Resevre Bank the data is likely to push them towards a February easing, rather than a March. We've got retail sales falling in trend terms for five consecutive months, which is unprecedented. We still have high real short-term interest rates and an unemployment rate that is rising in trend terms. On the basis of the inflation result, another 50 basis point cut in the official interest rate could be accomodated."
TIM PFITZNER, TREASURY ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"This confirms the story that both retailers and other business related to the industry have been telling us. We knew that this was going to be soft. We're in the camp that says we've hit the bottom of that (interest rate) cycle. Our concerns for rate cuts would still be wages, seeing the full impact on economic activity of the last cut."
NIGEL DOUGLAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH AUSTRALIA:

"Weaker than expected. It fitted in with anecdotal reports and company reports that we got in December. The numbers suggest that obviously the consumer cut back spending ... but because of the change in spending patterns (holding off purchases to post-Christmas sales) I wouldn't read too much into this. For the market this information probably boosts the chances of an easing."
